content: Obstetrics is a surgical specialty that focuses on the care of women and their offspring during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period (puerperium). The term originates from the Latin word obstare, meaning to stand by. Midwifery is the non-surgical counterpart to obstetrics. Most obstetricians are also gynecologists, and the combined field is referred to as obstetrics and gynecology. The average gestational period for humans is 40 weeks when calculated by gestational age and 38 weeks when calculated by fertilization age. Pregnancy is divided into three trimesters. Antenatal Care During pregnancy, an obstetrician or midwife regularly monitors the progress of the pregnancy, screens for new diseases, and manages preexisting conditions that may affect the pregnancy. The frequency of antenatal visits depends on the presence of risk factors, such as diabetes, and the availability of local resources. Key risk factors that must be systematically excluded, especially as pregnancy advances, include pre-eclampsia, abnormal placental placement, abnormal fetal presentation, and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). For example, pre-eclampsia is identified by monitoring blood pressure and testing for protein in the urine (albuminuria). Placenta previa, a condition where the placenta partially or completely obstructs the birth canal, is diagnosed using ultrasound and often necessitates elective cesarean delivery. Fetal presentation is assessed in late pregnancy, with the normal presentation being cephalic (head-first). Abnormal presentations include breech (feet or buttocks first), transverse (side-on), or oblique (angled). IUGR refers to a fetus that is smaller than expected for its gestational age, with growth parameters falling below the 10th percentile on a fetal growth chart. Causes of IUGR can be intrinsic (fetal) or extrinsic (maternal or placental issues). Signs and Symptoms by Trimester First Trimester: Elevated levels of β-hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) can cause morning sickness, fatigue, mood swings, and food cravings. These symptoms typically resolve by 12 to 16 weeks of gestation. Second Trimester: The abdomen becomes visibly enlarged as the uterus rises from the pelvis. Hyperpigmentation, such as the linea nigra, may appear. Third Trimester: The mother may experience backaches due to changes in spinal curvature to accommodate weight distribution. Mild urinary incontinence may occur due to bladder compression by the uterus. Heartburn is also common due to stomach compression. General Physical Signs Bluish discoloration of the vagina and cervix (Chadwick's sign). Softening and cyanosis of the cervix after 4 weeks (Goodell's sign). Softening of the uterus after 6 weeks (Hegar's or Ladin's sign). Breast swelling and tenderness. Linea nigra (a dark line from the umbilicus to the pubis). Telangiectasias and palmar erythema. Amenorrhea, nausea, vomiting, and breast pain. Fetal movement and sciatica (pain from sciatic nerve compression). Maternal Physiology Pregnancy induces significant physiological changes in the cardiovascular, hematologic, metabolic, renal, and respiratory systems to support the growing fetus and prepare for delivery. Cardiovascular Changes Plasma and blood volume increase by 40-50% to meet the demands of the fetus. Heart rate increases by approximately 15 beats per minute, and cardiac output rises by about 50%, primarily during the first trimester. Systemic vascular resistance decreases due to progesterone-induced smooth muscle relaxation, leading to a drop in blood pressure, which normalizes by 36 weeks. Persistent hypertension beyond this point warrants investigation for pre-eclampsia. Hematologic Changes Plasma volume increases by 50%, while red blood cell volume increases by only 20-30%, resulting in a decrease in hematocrit. White blood cell count rises and may exceed 20,000/mL under stress. Platelet concentration decreases to the lower end of normal (100-150 million/mL). Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state due to increased production of coagulation factors, particularly fibrinogen and factor VIII. Metabolic Changes Protein metabolism is altered, with an additional kilogram of protein deposited, half of which supports fetal and placental growth, and the other half supports uterine, breast, and plasma protein development. Prenatal vitamins, including folic acid (8 mg/day), are recommended to prevent neural tube defects. Omega-3 fatty acids and choline supplementation are beneficial for fetal brain and visual development. Gastrointestinal Changes Nausea and vomiting (morning sickness) are linked to elevated β-hCG levels and typically resolve by 14-16 weeks. Gastric emptying time is prolonged, and decreased gastroesophageal sphincter tone can lead to acid reflux. Reduced colonic motility increases water absorption, contributing to constipation. Renal Changes Kidney and ureter size increase, and the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) rises by 50%, normalizing around 20 weeks postpartum. Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels decrease, while glucosuria may occur due to tubular reabsorption saturation. Persistent glucosuria may indicate gestational diabetes. The renin-angiotensin system is upregulated, increasing aldosterone levels, but plasma sodium remains unchanged due to the compensatory increase in GFR. Pulmonary Changes Tidal volume increases by 30-40%, while total lung capacity decreases by 5% due to diaphragmatic elevation. Expiratory reserve volume decreases, and minute ventilation increases by 30-40%, leading to reduced PaCO2 and compensated respiratory alkalosis. These changes may contribute to dyspnea. Endocrine Changes Estrogen levels rise, primarily produced by the placenta, and are associated with fetal well-being. Progesterone production increases, initially by the corpus luteum and later by the placenta, promoting smooth muscle relaxation. Human placental lactogen (hPL) ensures nutrient supply to the fetus, induces lipolysis, and acts as an insulin antagonist, contributing to a diabetogenic effect. Prolactin and alkaline phosphatase levels also increase. Musculoskeletal and Dermatological Changes Lower back pain results from a shift in the center of gravity. Elevated estrogen levels can cause spider angiomas and palmar erythema. Increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) leads to hyperpigmentation of the nipples, umbilicus, abdominal midline (linea nigra), perineum, and face (melasma or chloasma). Prenatal Care Routine prenatal care includes physical exams, laboratory tests, and imaging to monitor maternal and fetal health. Key tests include: First Trimester: Complete blood count (CBC), blood type, antibody screen, rubella immunity, syphilis screening, hepatitis B antigen, gonorrhea and chlamydia cultures, tuberculosis testing, Pap smear, urinalysis, and HIV screening. Second Trimester: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) or triple screen, ultrasound, and amniocentesis for older patients. Third Trimester: Hematocrit, glucose tolerance testing for gestational diabetes, and group B streptococcus screening. Imaging Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality during pregnancy due to its safety and real-time capabilities. It is used to confirm intrauterine pregnancy, estimate gestational age, assess fetal growth, and detect anomalies. Key scans are performed at 12 weeks (dating scan) and 20 weeks (detailed anomaly scan). Emergencies in Obstetrics Ectopic Pregnancy: Implantation of the embryo outside the uterus, often in the fallopian tube, can cause life-threatening internal bleeding. Pre-eclampsia: A hypertensive disorder characterized by high blood pressure and proteinuria. Severe cases may progress to eclampsia, involving seizures, which can be fatal. Definitions Embryo: Conceptus from fertilization to 10 weeks of gestation. Fetus: From 10 weeks of gestation to birth. Infant: From birth to 1 year of age. Gestational Age: Time from the last menstrual period to the present. Trimester Definitions: First (up to 14 weeks), second (14-28 weeks), third (28 weeks to delivery). Viability: The minimum age for fetal survival, typically in the third trimester.
